transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came because… people been talking, you know, over at the domino table, and sometimes even the man on the radio, they say little things that feel like they’re meant for me. Not everybody catches it. My wife, she says, “Oh, that’s just talk,” but she says that about a lot of things—like when the neighbor’s dog barked all night, she said it was nothing too.

But these messages, they’re warnings, I think. Like I’m supposed to be careful. That’s why I’m here.
Have you ever heard a voice speaking when no one else was there?

Yes… yes, I have. Mostly in the afternoons, when the house gets real quiet. I’ll hear my old friend call my name from out on the porch, clear as if he’s standing there. Sometimes it’s not words, just him humming one of them choir songs we used to know.

Funny thing, he always had a strong voice in church—could carry right over everybody. But, uh… yes, I do hear it, even when nobody’s there.
Is that old friend whose voice you hear still alive?

I don’t rightly know if he’s still alive now… we fell out of touch a long while back. But the voice, it sounds just like him. Some afternoons, when the house gets quiet, I hear him call my name from the porch, or hum one of them choir songs, clear like he’s standing right there. Choir music sticks with you, you know… them old songs.
When you hear your old friend, does the voice seem to come from outside you, like from the porch or the radio, or does it feel more like it is inside your head?

It feels like it’s coming from outside me, like out on the porch. I’ll be sitting there and hear him call my name, or sometimes humming one of them choir songs, clear like he’s standing right there.

Those old songs, you know, they stay in your bones… we used to sing them way back. But yes, doctor, it don’t feel like it’s just in my head. It sounds like it’s out there.
Has a doctor ever told you that you have a brain illness or nerve problem, like dementia, Parkinson’s disease, or seizures?

I don’t think so… not that I remember, anyway. Doctors say a lot of things when you get to my age, and I don’t always keep all them names straight.

My cousin had something with his shaking hands, years back—couldn’t hardly button his shirt—but me, I don’t recall anybody telling me I had one of those brain or nerve illnesses. If they did, they didn’t explain it in a way that stuck with me.
Did these warnings and the voice start all of a sudden?

Not all of a sudden, no… least I don’t think so. It sort of came and went at first.

The voice and those warnings, them special messages, they been happening on and off maybe… about nine months now. Hard to pin it exact, because one month runs into the next when you’re old and not working anymore. I remember thinking it was around when the weather was changing, but then again I get mixed up on seasons sometimes. But no, it wasn’t just one day out of nowhere and then constant. More like it started and kept coming back.
Have you been having trouble with your memory?

My memory? Well… I don’t know. I forget little things sometimes, like where I set my glasses, but everybody does that, don’t they?

Now my sister, she used to say I could remember hymns from when we were children better than what I had for breakfast. Funny thing, those old songs stick with you… but as for trouble trouble with memory, I’m not sure what you mean exactly. I haven’t noticed anything big, I don’t think.
Have you been getting more confused lately than you used to?

More confused… I don’t know that I’d say more, no. I have my moments where I walk into a room and think, “Now what’d I come in here for?” but my mother used to do that too, and she’d laugh and say the doorway stole her thought.

I mean, I can get turned around if there’s too much going on, people talking over each other, that sort of thing. But lately more than before? I’m not real sure. Nobody’s sat me down and said, “You’re getting confused,” if that’s what you mean.
Have you been feeling less interested in being around other people than you used to?

Well… I still love my family, don’t get me wrong. I like knowing they’re around. But some days I just don’t have the push to be with folks much.

I’ll sit at the kitchen table a long while, not saying hardly anything, just looking out. Used to fool with the garden more, and choir practice too… I always liked the old hymns, especially the ones with a good bass line, you know. My uncle used to sing so loud he’d shake the pew. But lately those things just go on without me, and I don’t feel much like getting up and going.
Do you believe anyone is doing something physically impossible to control you, like putting thoughts into your mind or taking them out?

I don’t know about somebody putting thoughts in or taking them out, not like that exactly. But… the reason I came, Doctor, is those men at the domino table, they’ll say little things, and I can tell it’s meant for me. And sometimes the radio announcer too, just a word here or there, like a warning.

My wife says, “That’s just talk, you’re hearing things in it,” but I know when a message is for me. They’re telling me to be careful. Funny, I used to play dominoes with my cousin every Saturday—he’d slap those tiles down like he was mad at the table—but this is different. It’s not just regular talking.
Before these warnings and voices began, did you have a stroke?

A stroke? I… I don’t know. Nobody told me I had one, least not that I remember.

My old neighbor had one, you know, and his face kind of—well, you could see it. Folks brought casseroles for a week. But with me, before all this started, I can’t say there was something like that. I’m not real sure what counts, though.
Have you been speaking much less than you used to?

Yes… I suppose I have. I don’t mean to be rude to anybody. I still love my family, I do. But a lot of days I’m just sitting there at the kitchen table, not saying much of anything.

My wife’ll be moving around, maybe asking me something, and I’ll answer short, or not right away. I used to talk more, especially after choir practice—those old songs would get in my head. And the garden too, I could tell you about tomatoes all afternoon. Now I just kind of let it all go by and don’t feel like opening my mouth much.
Has anyone close to you told you that your memory has been getting worse?

I don’t think so… not that anybody’s sat me down and said, “Your memory’s going bad.” My wife might fuss if I forget where I put my glasses, but everybody does that, don’t they?

I mean, I used to keep track of all kinds of things—who owed who a dollar after dominoes, when the tomatoes needed watering. Tomatoes are funny, you miss one day in the heat and they just sulk on you. But no, I can’t say anyone close to me has told me my memory is getting worse.
Has any doctor ever told you that you have Parkinson’s disease?

Parkinson’s… no, I don’t believe any doctor’s ever told me that. I’ve heard of it—there was a man at church, his hands shook some, and he always sat near the back because he didn’t like folks looking at him. Nice man.

But me, no… nobody in a white coat has said, “You have Parkinson’s,” not that I remember.
Before these warnings and voices started, did you have a serious illness or injury?

I’m not sure I’d call anything serious, doctor. I mean, I’ve had my share of aches and colds and such—when you get to my age, seems like something’s always creaking. But before all that started… I don’t remember some big injury or illness right before it.

I did fall once years ago in the yard, but that was more me tripping over the hose. My wife told me to roll it up, and she was right about that. She’s usually right about those little things. But no, I don’t think there was anything serious like you mean.
Have you been having more trouble taking care of your usual day-to-day tasks than you used to?

Some, yes… I suppose more than I’d like to admit.

I used to be steady with my little routines. Choir on the right evening, garden watered and tied up, dominoes with the fellas. Lately I’ve missed choir rehearsals—just didn’t make it there, or got mixed up and then felt foolish. And the garden… well, parts of it have gone wild on me. Weeds don’t wait for a man to get himself together, you know.

And dominoes, I don’t go like I used to. I think I’ve made it uncomfortable a few times, or maybe folks got uneasy around me… hard to say. It used to be a good time, just slapping tiles and arguing over nothing. Now I mostly stay home.
Has your wife told you that you’ve been getting more forgetful lately?

My wife… well, she says a lot of things, you know, and most of them end up being right. She’ll tell me, “You left that cup there,” or “You already asked me that,” but I don’t know if she’s said I’m getting more forgetful exactly.

Sometimes she gets that look, though. Married long enough, you know the look. But then again, she’s always been sharper with keeping track of things—birthdays, bills, who brought what casserole to church. I was never much good at all that. So… I’m not sure. I’d have to ask her what she thinks.
Has your wife said that your memory has been getting worse?

I don’t know that she’s put it that way, exactly. She’ll fuss at me now and then—well, not fuss, more like remind me—and sometimes I think she’s just tired, because she keeps track of everything in that house.

I mean, she remembers where the little scissors are, which drawer has the batteries, all that. I never could keep up with those things even when I was younger. So… has she said my memory’s getting worse? I’m not real sure she’s said those words.
Has your wife told you that your memory has been getting worse?

I… I don’t know, doctor. I know you asked me that, and I’m trying to think of the exact thing she said, because my wife is particular with words sometimes.

She’ll say things around the house, you know—“Didn’t I tell you that already?” or “You put that over there instead of here”—but whether she’s come right out and said, “Your memory is getting worse,” I can’t rightly say.

And my wife, she’s always kept the household straight. Even back when the kids were little, she could remember whose lunchbox was whose and what day the church supper was. I’d be standing there with my hat in my hand, just waiting to be told where to go. So… I’m not sure if this is new, or if she’s just noticing more.
Do you ever get lost in places that used to be familiar to you?

Getting lost… no, I don’t think so. I mean, I don’t go as many places as I used to. My wife does most of the figuring if we’re going somewhere, and these roads have changed so much—new stores where the old ones were, stoplights they put in after I was already used to things.

But places I know, like around home or church, I can usually tell where I am. Sometimes I’ll take a minute, you know, look around and get my bearings. That used to happen when I was young too, especially if somebody’s talking at me while I’m trying to think.

So… lost, like not knowing where I am? I don’t recall that happening.

I don’t know that she’s put it that way, exactly. She’ll fuss at me now and then—well, not fuss, more like remind me—and sometimes I think she’s just tired, because she keeps track of everything in that house.

I mean, she remembers where the little scissors are, which drawer has the batteries, all that. I never could keep up with those things even when I was younger. So… has she said my memory’s getting worse? I’m not real sure she’s said those words.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know, doctor. I know you asked me that, and I’m trying to think of the exact thing she said, because my wife is particular with words sometimes.

She’ll say things around the house, you know—“Didn’t I tell you that already?” or “You put that over there instead of here”—but whether she’s come right out and said, “Your memory is getting worse,” I can’t rightly say.

And my wife, she’s always kept the household straight. Even back when the kids were little, she could remember whose lunchbox was whose and what day the church supper was. I’d be standing there with my hat in my hand, just waiting to be told where to go. So… I’m not sure if this is new, or if she’s just noticing more.

patient.answer:
Getting lost… no, I don’t think so. I mean, I don’t go as many places as I used to. My wife does most of the figuring if we’re going somewhere, and these roads have changed so much—new stores where the old ones were, stoplights they put in after I was already used to things.

But places I know, like around home or church, I can usually tell where I am. Sometimes I’ll take a minute, you know, look around and get my bearings. That used to happen when I was young too, especially if somebody’s talking at me while I’m trying to think.

So… lost, like not knowing where I am? I don’t recall that happening.
